title: Jesus Knew Judas Would Betray Him — And Still Washed His Feet
paragraphs:
Jesus Knew Judas Would Betray Him — And Still Washed His Feet
The Night Love Knelt Before the Man Who Would Sell It
There are moments in Scripture that do not simply tell us what Jesus did.
They reveal who He is.
And perhaps one of the most shocking pictures of Christ’s heart is not found when He healed the sick, calmed the storm, raised the dead, or fed thousands.
It is found in a quiet room.
A basin.
A towel.
A group of disciples.
And one man sitting among them who had already decided to betray Him.
The most beautiful act of humility in human history happened with betrayal sitting only a few feet away.
Jesus knew.
He knew the hands He was washing would soon guide soldiers to arrest Him.
He knew the feet He was cleaning would walk into the night carrying a betrayal worth thirty pieces of silver.
He knew Judas’ kiss would not be a kiss of affection, but a signal of destruction.
And still…
Jesus knelt.
That is the scandal of grace.
That is the heart of a Savior who does not love people because they deserve love.
He loves because love is who He is.
The Gospel of John captures this breathtaking moment:

“Jesus knew that the Father had put all things under his power, and that he had come from God and was returning to God; so he got up from the meal, took off his outer clothing, and wrapped a towel around his waist.”
— John 13:3-4 (NIV)
Notice what John tells us before Jesus washes feet.
Jesus knew who He was.
He knew where He came from.
He knew where He was going.
And because He knew His identity, He was free to serve.
Pride needs recognition.
Insecurity needs approval.
But Jesus, completely secure in the glory of heaven, lowered Himself to the position of a servant.
The Greek word used for “took” or “laid aside” His outer clothing is connected to the idea of intentionally setting something down. Jesus was not losing His authority.
He was demonstrating it.
The King was not becoming less because He served.
He was revealing what true greatness actually looks like.

“For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
— Mark 10:45
The world says greatness is being above others.
Jesus showed greatness by getting below them.
And then comes the part that should stop every heart.
Judas was there.
The same Judas who would betray Him.
John writes:
— John 13:26
In ancient Jewish culture, sharing bread and offering a dipped piece of food was an act of fellowship and honor.
Jesus was not accidentally loving Judas.
He was intentionally loving Judas.
Even at the final moment before betrayal, Jesus extended kindness.
This is the mystery of divine love.
Christ was not unaware of Judas’ darkness.
He was fully aware.
The Greek word for “betray” used throughout the New Testament is παραδίδωμι (paradidōmi), meaning “to hand over” or “deliver up.”
Judas would hand Jesus over to His enemies.
But before Judas handed Jesus over to the world, Jesus had already offered Himself for the world.
The betrayal did not surprise Him.
The cross was not Plan B.
The Lamb of God walked toward suffering willingly.

“As the Father knows me and I know the Father—and I lay down my life for the sheep.”
— John 10:15
Jesus did not lose His life.
He gave it.
That changes everything.
Because if Jesus could wash Judas’ feet…
what does that mean for you?
For the person who feels too far gone?
For the person carrying shame from yesterday?
For the person who wonders if God is tired of their failures?
For the person who has hidden parts of their life because they believe God would reject them if He truly knew?
Here is the shocking truth:
He already knows.
He knows the thoughts you never say out loud.
He knows the battles nobody sees.
He knows the places where you have fallen.
He knows every scar, every mistake, every regret.
And yet the same Jesus who knew Judas would betray Him still walked toward Judas with a towel.
Because Jesus does not love the future version of you after you become perfect.
He loves you while He is transforming you.
Grace does not ignore sin.
Grace defeats sin.
The same hands that washed Judas’ feet were later pierced because of human sin.
The same Savior who knelt in humility would soon stand before His accusers in silence.
The same Jesus who served the man who betrayed Him would die for the very people who rejected Him.
That is why the cross is so offensive to human pride.
Because it tells us we cannot save ourselves.
But it is also the greatest hope humanity has ever received.
Because the God we ran from came looking for us.
The prophet Isaiah wrote:

“But he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.”
— Isaiah 53:5
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that good people found God.
But that God came searching for broken people.
Not that we cleaned ourselves before approaching Jesus.
But that Jesus came into our mess and made us clean.
Peter experienced this same humility when he initially resisted Jesus washing his feet.

“Jesus answered, ‘Unless I wash you, you have no share with me.’”
— John 13:8
Peter wanted to follow Jesus.
But he struggled to receive from Jesus.
And many of us do the same.
We want to serve God, but we struggle to admit we need His grace.
We want to look strong, but God invites us to surrender.
We want to hide our wounds, but Christ invites us to healing.
The towel reminds us of something powerful:
Before Jesus asks us to serve others, He asks us to let Him serve us.
Before we wash feet, we must allow Him to wash our hearts.
Maybe you have felt like Judas.
Maybe you have betrayed your own values.
Maybe you have promised God you would change and then returned to the same chains.
Maybe you have wondered whether Jesus could still want you after everything you have done.
Look again at that room.
Jesus knew Judas.
And Jesus still loved Judas.
That does not mean Judas’ betrayal was acceptable.
It means Christ’s love was greater than Judas’ failure.
But there is also a warning.
Judas was close to Jesus physically but never surrendered his heart.
He walked with Jesus but never truly belonged to Him.
The greatest danger is not being far from religion.
The greatest danger is being near Jesus but refusing to surrender.
The question is not simply, “Have you heard about Jesus?”
The question is:
“Have you given yourself to Jesus?”
Because the same Christ who washes feet will one day return as King.
The same Savior who offers mercy today will judge with righteousness tomorrow.
Today is the invitation.
Today is the moment to stop hiding.
Today is the moment to bring the betrayal, the shame, the secret places, the broken pieces, and lay them before the One whose hands were pierced for you.
Jesus knew Judas would betray Him.
And Jesus still washed his feet.
Because Jesus does not wait for people to become worthy before He shows love.
He loves, He calls, He forgives, and He transforms.
This is why we call it:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Someone reading this right now needs the reminder that God has not abandoned them. Share this with them.
Because someone you know may be one message away from remembering that their failure is not greater than the mercy of Jesus.
The feet Jesus washed were dusty, flawed, and destined to stumble — and He still knelt, because grace was never about how clean we could become, but how far Christ was willing to come.
